post_text:
I believed our blue-green database migration was completely foolproof because our dual-write abstraction handled deduplication directly in application code.

I relied on soft Java-level locks instead of strict target schema rules to prevent double-inserts during the shadow phase.

Peak load hit on Monday morning, forcing the JVM into prolonged garbage collection pauses under intense memory pressure.

The stop-the-world freeze suspended local lock validation just long enough for parallel threads to bypass the check and bombard the target database simultaneously.

Within minutes, duplicate financial records flooded the primary ledger, silently corrupting downstream relational dependencies.

I assumed my clever thread synchronization would gracefully bridge the legacy schema to the new architecture.

Instead, I had traded away hard, boring database constraints for transient memory-based guarantees, leaving the write path helpless when the runtime drifted.

What I learned:

Application logic cannot guarantee data integrity during a migration; only immutable database constraints protect the destination state.
